title: Acute Cough Assessment
summary: A clinician-facing prompt for assessing acute cough, distinguishing viral upper-respiratory infection from serious lower-respiratory pathology, and supporting diagnosis, investigation and safety-netting.

sections.title: Assessment priorities
sections.intro: Use this guide as a prompt. It does not replace clinical judgement, local pathways or urgent escalation when serious pathology is suspected.

items.title: Must confirm or exclude
mustConfirmOrExclude: Airway compromise, severe respiratory distress or hypoxia.
Pneumonia (fever, crackles, consolidation, raised inflammatory markers).
Pulmonary embolism risk and symptoms (unilateral leg swelling, chest pain, haemoptysis).
Acute asthma exacerbation or COPD decompensation.
Pertussis or other serious respiratory infection (immunisation status, whooping, paroxysms).
Foreign body or aspiration risk.
Acute cardiac cause (heart failure, acute coronary syndrome).
Immunosuppression or comorbidity increasing infection risk.
items.importantLimitation: Absence of fever, focal signs or abnormal chest X-ray does not exclude pneumonia. Normal oxygen saturation does not exclude serious pathology.

sections.title: Focused history
sections.intro: Characterise the cough pattern, associated symptoms and risk factors for serious causes.

items.title: Cough characteristics and pattern
mustConfirmOrExclude: Onset: sudden, gradual or insidious; duration (hours, days, weeks).
Pattern: dry vs. productive; frequency and severity; worse at night or with activity.
Sputum: colour, blood-staining, volume, consistency.
Associated: shortness of breath, wheeze, stridor, hoarseness or voice change.

items.title: Systemic and constitutional symptoms
mustConfirmOrExclude: Fever, rigors, night sweats or chills.
Malaise, fatigue, myalgia or headache.
Nausea, vomiting, diarrhoea or abdominal pain.
Chest pain or pleuritic discomfort.
Recent upper-respiratory infection, sick contacts or relevant exposures.

items.title: Red-flag features in history
mustConfirmOrExclude: Significant dyspnoea, orthopnoea or paroxysmal nocturnal dyspnoea.
Haemoptysis (coughing up blood).
Unilateral leg swelling or recent immobility (DVT/PE risk).
Chest pain with exertion or at rest.
Weight loss, night sweats or prolonged cough (>3 weeks).
Immunosuppression, pregnancy or recent surgery.
Known asthma, COPD, heart failure or malignancy.

sections.title: Serious pathology screen
sections.intro: Positive features should change disposition and trigger appropriate investigation or referral.

items.title: Respiratory emergency
urgentFeatures: Severe respiratory distress, stridor, inability to speak in sentences, or SpO₂ <92%.
Sudden onset severe dyspnoea or acute deterioration in known lung disease.
Signs of airway obstruction or foreign body aspiration.
implications: Immediate emergency assessment and possible hospital admission.

items.title: Community-acquired pneumonia
urgentFeatures: Fever with cough and focal chest signs (crackles, dullness, bronchial breathing).
CRP >100 mg/L, raised white-cell count or focal infiltrate on chest X-ray.
Severe systemic illness, confusion or significant functional decline.
implications: Chest X-ray and same-day assessment; hospital referral likely.

items.title: Pulmonary embolism
urgentFeatures: Acute dyspnoea with unilateral leg swelling or recent immobility.
Tachycardia, hypotension or signs of shock.
Risk factors: recent surgery, malignancy, thrombophilia or oral contraceptives.
implications: Urgent hospital assessment and imaging (CT pulmonary angiography).

items.title: Acute asthma exacerbation
urgentFeatures: Known asthma with acute onset wheeze and dyspnoea.
Inability to speak in sentences, peak flow <50% predicted, or SpO₂ <92%.
Silent chest, inability to cough or signs of respiratory fatigue.
implications: Immediate bronchodilators and steroid therapy; hospital referral if severe.

sections.title: Focused examination
sections.intro: Examine for respiratory distress, focal findings and signs of serious systemic illness.

items.title: General appearance and vital signs
howToTest: Assess overall appearance, distress and ability to speak.
Record temperature, heart rate, respiratory rate, blood pressure and oxygen saturation.
Note signs of cyanosis, pallor or respiratory difficulty.
normal: Clinically well, speaking in full sentences, SpO₂ ≥95% on room air.
abnormal: Respiratory distress, dyspnoea at rest, SpO₂ <92%, fever >38.5°C, tachycardia.
implications: Abnormal vital signs or distress mandate further investigation and possible escalation.

items.title: Lung and chest examination
howToTest: Inspect for symmetry, use of accessory muscles and signs of distress.
Palpate for tracheal deviation and fremitus.
Percuss both lung fields for dullness.
Auscultate: note breath sounds, crackles, wheeze, rhonchi.
normal: Bilateral equal breath sounds, no added sounds, normal resonance.
abnormal: Focal crackles (pneumonia), wheeze (asthma/COPD), reduced air entry, dullness (consolidation).
implications: Focal signs suggest lower-respiratory infection; diffuse wheeze suggests obstructive airway disease.

items.title: Cardiovascular assessment
howToTest: Assess JVP, peripheral perfusion and signs of heart failure (orthopnoea, oedema).
Examine legs for swelling, calf tenderness or signs of DVT.
normal: Regular heart rate, no murmur, normal JVP, no peripheral oedema or leg swelling.
abnormal: Tachycardia, new murmur, raised JVP, oedema, unilateral leg swelling.
implications: Cardiac findings suggest heart failure or arrhythmia; leg swelling raises PE risk.

sections.title: Common clinical patterns
sections.intro: Pattern recognition supports diagnosis but does not replace systematic assessment.

items.title: Viral upper-respiratory infection
commonFindings: Gradual onset; dry or minimally productive cough.
Nasal congestion, sore throat, mild fever or no fever.
No focal chest signs; normal chest X-ray.
implications: Self-limiting viral infection; supportive care only. Antibiotics not indicated.

items.title: Community-acquired pneumonia
commonFindings: Fever, productive cough, shortness of breath.
Focal crackles or consolidation on examination.
CRP >50 mg/L or focal infiltrate on chest X-ray.
implications: Antibiotic therapy indicated; chest X-ray and severity assessment required.

items.title: Asthma or COPD exacerbation
commonFindings: Known asthma or COPD with acute onset dyspnoea and wheeze.
implications: Bronchodilators, corticosteroids and assessment of severity; hospital referral if severe.

items.title: Acute bronchitis
commonFindings: Normal chest examination and chest X-ray.
implications: Self-limiting; supportive care. Antibiotics not indicated unless superimposed infection.

sections.title: Management and disposition
sections.intro: Base decisions on severity, investigation findings and ability for community follow-up.

items.title: Investigation
mustConfirmOrExclude: Chest X-ray: indicated if pneumonia suspected, fever >38.5°C, focal signs or dyspnoea.
FBC/CRP: indicated if pneumonia suspected or severe systemic illness.
Peak flow: measure if asthma or COPD exacerbation suspected.
ECG or BNP: consider if heart failure or acute coronary syndrome suspected.

items.title: Community management is appropriate when
mustConfirmOrExclude: No red flags for serious pathology present.
SpO₂ ≥94% and respiratory rate normal.
Able to maintain fluids and oral treatment.
Reliable access to follow-up and escalation route.

items.title: Refer or admit for hospital assessment
urgentFeatures: Respiratory distress, SpO₂ <92%, stridor or signs of airway compromise.
Pneumonia with fever, systemic illness or comorbidity.
Severe asthma exacerbation not responding to initial treatment.
Suspected PE or other serious pathology.
Unable to maintain fluids or manage at home safely.
implications: Same-day hospital assessment or admission required.

items.title: Acute cough
safetyNetting: Call 999 or go to ED immediately for: severe difficulty breathing, stridor, inability to speak in sentences, SpO₂ <90%, severe chest pain, coughing up large amounts of blood, or signs of shock.

Contact your GP or go to ED same-day for: high fever (>38.5°C) with cough; focal chest signs or breathlessness; suspected pneumonia; suspected PE (leg swelling + dyspnoea); or worsening asthma/COPD despite treatment.
Speak to your GP if: cough persists beyond 3 weeks; cough is not improving after 1 week of treatment; you develop new symptoms; or you have concerns about underlying causes.
